title: The medium is the message: How neurometabolic entanglement generates conscious experience
summary: Most neuroscientific accounts of consciousness assume that conscious experience is constituted by the information conveyed between neurons. The physical-chemical details of the metabolic and physiological processes that convey this information are correspondingly presumed to be relevant only insofar as they support the organization of information processes. We describe an alternative perspective that denies this presumed independence of the processing of neural information and the metabolic-physiological details of these processes. We call this alternative paradigm the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME). NME proposes that mental experience exemplifies the inseparability of the organization of neural information processes from the constraints imposed by the material-energetic properties of the neural medium itself. Central to this account is a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles patterns of forebrain information processing with midbrain regulatory systems that modulate forebrain metabolism. This enables patterns of neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying these information processes. It also constitutes a bottleneck that integrates diverse neural processes into an adaptively relevant unitary experience organized in terms of the global redistribution of metabolic support. Computational models of neural function cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; our proposed Möbius-like loop of neuro-metabolic entanglement offers a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism. Recognizing this entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the so-called "hard problem" of consciousness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME), arguing that conscious experience cannot be explained by neural information processing alone but arises from the inseparable entanglement of information organization with the material-energetic constraints of the neural medium, mediated by a recursive Möbius-like loop linking forebrain processing and midbrain metabolic regulation.
AI.motivation: Mainstream neuroscience assumes consciousness is constituted solely by information conveyed between neurons, treating metabolic and physiological details as mere background support. The authors challenge this presumed independence of information processing from the physical-chemical substrate.
AI.method: A conceptual/theoretical framework: the authors describe an alternative paradigm (NME) centered on a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles forebrain information processing patterns with midbrain regulatory systems modulating forebrain metabolism, enabling activity to indirectly redistribute metabolic resources and acting as a bottleneck that integrates diverse processes into a unified experience.
AI.result: The theory implies that computational models cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; instead, neural activity should be modeled as dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism.
AI.conclusion: Recognizing this neuro-metabolic entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap of the "hard problem" of consciousness and offers a framework for future models in which neural activity and metabolism are mutually and recursively coupled.

title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
comment: Accepted (non-archival) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops Sim2Science and Interp4Discovery. Code: https://github.com/Shrivatsa-Deshmukh/sbi-gate-vs-ablation
summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

AI.tldr: Learned feature gates in simulation-based inference (NPE) do not reflect feature importance; gate weights were negatively correlated with ablation-based importance across nine seeds, warning against interpreting them as causal importance measures.
AI.motivation: SBI fits mechanistic models but gives little insight into which data features shape inferred parameters, so cheap interpretability methods appear useful. Feature gates are a candidate low-cost approach, but they rely on the assumption that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance — an assumption this paper tests.
AI.method: In a computational neuroscience setting, neural posterior estimation inferred four physiological parameters of a Jansen-Rit model of interacting neuronal populations. Two jointly trained gates were examined (independent sigmoid weights, competing softmax weights), and gate-based importance was compared with a retrain-based ablation benchmark (each feature removed and NPE retrained) across nine independent training seeds.
AI.result: Gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho ≈ -0.61 for sigmoid, -0.56 for softmax). Total signal power, the most important feature by ablation, was among those the gates down-weighted most, while gating cost negligible predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The findings extend a pattern observed for attention mechanisms in NLP and EEG explainability to SBI, suggesting caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

title: Modelling Toxin-Induced Intraspecific Personality Variation in Predator-Prey Dynamics
comment: 38 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Journal of Theoretical Biology
summary: Personality traits, such as boldness and shyness, can affect interspecific interactions through differences in individual behaviour. Environmental toxins may also alter these traits. However, few predator-prey models have considered animal personality. In this study, we extend a toxin-dependent predator-prey model by incorporating personality variation in both prey and predators. Prey personality affects birth and growth, whereas predator personality affects the predator functional response. The model is parameterized for rainbow trout and aquatic insect prey exposed to methylmercury. Numerical results show that prey and predator personality have different effects on population dynamics. Prey personality tends to reduce biomass fluctuations and promote stable coexistence. In contrast, predator personality can increase biomass fluctuations and lead to persistent population oscillations. These effects are mainly observed at low and intermediate toxin concentrations that are environmentally relevant to freshwater ecosystems. Using a quasi-steady-state approximation, we reduce the model to a two-dimensional system and study its positivity, boundedness, and the existence of equilibria. The equilibrium structure depends jointly on the toxin level and the prey and predator personality contrasts. Based on this existence classification, we numerically investigate the local stability of all feasible equilibria and identify parameter regions corresponding to locally stable extinction, prey-only persistence, coexistence, and bistability. Overall, toxin-induced personality variation can qualitatively change predator-prey dynamics.

AI.tldr: A toxin-dependent predator-prey model is extended to include personality variation in both prey (birth/growth) and predators (functional response); personality contrasts qualitatively reshape stability, coexistence, and bistability mainly at low-to-intermediate methylmercury levels.
AI.motivation: Personality traits like boldness and shyness shape interspecific interactions, and environmental toxins may alter these traits, yet few predator-prey models account for animal personality. The authors aim to understand how toxin-induced personality variation jointly affects prey and predator population dynamics.
AI.method: They extend a toxin-dependent predator-prey model by adding personality variation: prey personality affects birth and growth, predator personality affects the functional response. The model is parameterized for rainbow trout and aquatic insect prey exposed to methylmercury. A quasi-steady-state approximation reduces it to a 2D system, for which positivity, boundedness, and equilibrium existence are analyzed; local stability of feasible equilibria and parameter regions for extinction, prey-only persistence, coexistence, and bistability are then studied numerically.
AI.result: Prey and predator personality have opposite effects: prey personality reduces biomass fluctuations and promotes stable coexistence, whereas predator personality increases fluctuations and can drive persistent oscillations. These effects appear mainly at low and intermediate, environmentally relevant toxin concentrations. The equilibrium structure depends jointly on toxin level and prey/predator personality contrasts.
AI.conclusion: Toxin-induced personality variation can qualitatively change predator-prey dynamics, so personality should be incorporated when assessing ecotoxicological impacts on population stability and persistence.

title: Shorter but not more catalytic: an active-site-resolved model of how tau reshapes amyloid-$β$ secondary nucleation
summary: Tau cross-seeding creates a mechanistic puzzle. Tau fibrils accelerate amyloid-$β$42 (A$β$42) nucleation and produce a larger population of shorter A$β$ fibrils, yet homotypic secondary nucleation occurs at rare catalytic sites rather than uniformly over fibril mass. Does making more, shorter fibrils make the A$β$ population more catalytic? A coupled tau-A$β$ model is extended to track fibril number, fibril mass, total active secondary-nucleation sites, and the fraction of sites exposed after plaque consolidation. The model recovers the preceding plaque-surface-limited formulation when active sites form in direct proportion to fibril mass. At matched fibril mass, shortening alone has little effect: the departure of active-site density from mass proportionality scales inversely with mean fibril size, so the extra fibrils matter only if each birth event introduces about as many sites as elongation adds over a mean-length fibril. At equal time, the sign of the homotypic response is controlled mainly by a Damkohler number comparing monomer consumption by elongation with monomer clearance. Tau coupling increases homotypic secondary nucleation while clearance controls free monomer, but suppresses it once elongation becomes the dominant monomer sink. In a composite scenario, these regimes occur in sequence. Across all cases examined, including 800 Latin-hypercube samples and simulations with mean fibril lengths of 0.3-30 $μm$, direct tau catalysis increases accumulated oligomer-equivalent exposure. The model predicts that shorter tau-seeded fibrils are not intrinsically more catalytic unless their sites are more numerous per unit mass, more active, or more exposed; matched-mass site counting and secondary-nucleation measurements can distinguish these alternatives.

AI.tldr: A coupled tau-Aβ kinetic model shows that producing more, shorter Aβ fibrils does not intrinsically make the Aβ population more catalytic; the homotypic secondary-nucleation response depends on active-site density per unit mass and on a Damköhler number balancing elongation-driven monomer consumption against clearance.
AI.motivation: Tau cross-seeding accelerates Aβ42 nucleation and yields more, shorter Aβ fibrils, but homotypic secondary nucleation is known to occur at rare catalytic sites rather than uniformly across fibril mass. It is unclear whether simply having more, shorter fibrils makes the Aβ population more catalytic—a mechanistic puzzle linking fibril fragmentation, active-site availability, and plaque consolidation.
AI.method: An existing coupled tau-Aβ model is extended to explicitly track fibril number, fibril mass, total active secondary-nucleation sites, and the fraction of sites left exposed after plaque consolidation. The model reduces to a prior plaque-surface-limited formulation when active sites scale in proportion to fibril mass. Analyses include matched-mass comparisons, mean fibril lengths of 0.3–30 μm, a dimensionless Damköhler number (elongation vs. clearance), and 800 Latin-hypercube parameter samples.
AI.result: At matched fibril mass, shortening alone has little effect: deviation of active-site density from mass proportionality scales inversely with mean fibril size, so extra fibrils matter only if each birth event introduces roughly as many sites as elongation adds over a mean-length fibril. At equal time, the sign of the homotypic response is governed mainly by the Damköhler number: tau coupling raises homotypic secondary nucleation while clearance controls free monomer, but suppresses it once elongation dominates monomer consumption; in a composite scenario these regimes occur sequentially. Across all cases, direct tau catalysis increases accumulated oligomer-equivalent exposure.
AI.conclusion: Shorter tau-seeded fibrils are not intrinsically more catalytic unless their active sites are more numerous per unit mass, more active, or more exposed. Matched-mass site counting combined with secondary-nucleation measurements can distinguish these alternative mechanisms.

title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary appendices (32 pages) are included as an ancillary file. Code, exact input fixtures and saved run records: https://github.com/Haotian-Tang/recomb2027-pdd
summary:
Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost.
  On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources.
  We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it. The direction is a theorem at every error tolerance and held without exception in 23,545 draws, so which references are missing matters more than how many. Two adversarially chosen references suffice, at the median, to destroy uniqueness of the minimum explanation, and that number does not grow with panel size (Spearman 0.203, p = 0.15, over 20 to 353 references) where random loss scales linearly. Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%.
  That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. Published distance estimates exceed it in 296 of 296 cases. The mixture inferred by the published heuristic reproduces real observations better than the configuration that generated them in 282 of 296. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. It is unobservable through a point estimate of the count. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.

AI.tldr: The paper studies minimum-source deconvolution of phylogenetic distances, gives an exact algorithm parameterized by source budget, proves W[1]-hardness with missing references, and shows the relevant threshold (tolerance) is measurable on real data, where published estimates often exceed it.
AI.motivation: Understanding how few sources explain a mixture-to-reference distance profile, and how incomplete references affect this count, is central to interpreting phylogenetic distance deconvolution on real data. The authors want to characterize which references matter and whether the phenomenon is observable in practice.
AI.method: On a positive-rational reduced tree, an exact 2^O(K)·poly(B) bit-complexity algorithm for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves. W[1]-hardness proof for the case of arbitrary missing references with prescribed pendant. Empirical instrument: removing references can only lower the minimum source count; adversarial vs. random reference loss; a ground-truth-free error tolerance measure applied to a real 16S panel (10,575 references) and 296 published distance estimates.
AI.result: Direction of the monotonicity claim held in all 23,545 draws at every error tolerance. Two adversarial references suffice at the median to break uniqueness of the minimum explanation, and this does not scale with panel size (Spearman 0.203, p=0.15 over 20–353 references) while random loss scales linearly. Random removal of 7,931 of 10,575 references costs 1.8% of tolerance; comparable clade removal costs 90%. Published distance estimates exceed the tolerance in 296/296 cases; the published heuristic's mixture reproduces observations better than the generating configuration in 282/296.
AI.conclusion: Which references are missing matters more than how many. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice—it is unobservable through a point estimate of the count. The paper recommends that methods for this problem report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.

title: From Turing Patterns to Spike Self-Replication and Nucleation in a Growing-Domain Tulip Breaking Virus Model
summary: A recently proposed reaction-diffusion model for the tulip breaking virus (TBV) has been shown to generate striped pigmentation patterns on growing tulip petals. In this paper, we investigate the formation of localized spike patterns in this model in the asymptotic limit of small viral diffusivity. It is known that two distinct bifurcation mechanisms can occur which generate new spikes as the domain half-length $L$ slowly increases: spike self-replication and spike nucleation. Self-replication occurs through a saddle-node bifurcation of the inner spike core problem, whereas nucleation is associated with a fold of the nonlinear outer problem. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive critical conditions for these mechanisms and construct phase diagrams that predict which mechanism occurs first as $L$ increases, or whether nucleation is absent. We further combine these results with a Turing instability analysis of the homogeneous steady state to obtain a phase diagram of pattern-forming mechanisms. An interesting finding is that, for the TBV model, the Turing-unstable region lies entirely within the parameter regime where spike nucleation is possible. These results provide further insight into the mechanisms underlying the formation and evolution of pigmentation patterns in virus-infected tulips.

AI.tldr: This paper uses matched asymptotic expansions in the small-viral-diffusivity limit to analyze how localized spike patterns form in a reaction-diffusion model for tulip breaking virus, deriving critical conditions and phase diagrams that distinguish spike self-replication, spike nucleation, and Turing instability.
AI.motivation: A prior reaction-diffusion model for the tulip breaking virus reproduces striped petal pigmentation, but the mechanisms generating new localized spikes as the petal (domain half-length L) grows were not fully understood.
AI.method: Asymptotic analysis in the limit of small viral diffusivity using matched asymptotic expansions. Two bifurcation mechanisms are studied: spike self-replication (saddle-node bifurcation of the inner spike core problem) and spike nucleation (fold of the nonlinear outer problem). Critical conditions are derived, phase diagrams are constructed, and results are combined with a Turing instability analysis of the homogeneous steady state.
AI.result: Critical conditions for self-replication and nucleation are derived, yielding phase diagrams predicting which mechanism occurs first as L increases or whether nucleation is absent. Combined with Turing analysis, a phase diagram of pattern-forming mechanisms is obtained. Notably, for the TBV model the Turing-unstable region lies entirely within the parameter regime where spike nucleation is possible.
AI.conclusion: The analysis clarifies the mechanisms underlying formation and evolution of pigmentation patterns in virus-infected tulips, showing that Turing instability is nested within the nucleation-capable regime.

title: Music Between Two Minds: Individual Signatures, Shared States, and the Emergence of Creative Interaction
summary: Some of the most valued forms of human creativity arise between people-in conversation, collaboration, and improvised music-yet how two minds jointly regulate the flow of novelty in real time remains unknown. Here we examined the information dynamics of interpersonal improvisation using 986 professional jazz improvisations. Pitch-based fluctuations of uncertainty and surprise behaved as signatures of individual identity: the two partners differed within 90% of takes, performers were identifiable from single solos and the separation between partners persisted undiminished across turns and takes. Rhythm-based fluctuations showed the reverse organization: partners were statistically indistinguishable within a take yet shifted together from take to take, and this shared state drifted gradually as each performance progressed, with each performer moving away from their own past at the same rate as from their partner's. Beyond joint drift, solo hand-offs revealed turn-by-turn complementarity: when one performer exceeded their own average surprise in the predictive dynamics of improvisation, the partner's next solo fell below their own, in both pitch and rhythm and in all duos. Improvising pairs thus neither fuse into one system nor remain two independent ones: they preserve individual melodic voices while sharing a rhythmic state, within which moment-to-moment push-pull continually rebalances their interaction. Individuality and togetherness thus coexist, carried by different musical dimensions, a measurable organization of creativity that emerges between minds.

AI.tldr: In 986 professional jazz duo improvisations, pitch-based uncertainty/surprise fluctuations encoded individual identity, while rhythm-based fluctuations encoded a shared, drifting dyadic state; solo hand-offs showed turn-by-turn surprise complementarity across pitch and rhythm in all duos.
AI.motivation: Everyday creativity often emerges between people (conversation, collaboration, improvised music), yet how two minds jointly regulate the flow of novelty in real time is unknown. The paper asks how individuality and togetherness coexist during interpersonal improvisation.
AI.method: Analysis of information dynamics in 986 professional jazz duo improvisations: quantifying pitch- and rhythm-based fluctuations of uncertainty and surprise, testing performer identifiability within and across turns and takes, and examining solo hand-offs for turn-by-turn complementarity.
AI.result: Pitch fluctuations acted as individual signatures: partners differed in 90% of takes, performers were identifiable from single solos, and partner separation persisted undiminished across turns and takes. Rhythm fluctuations reversed this: partners were statistically indistinguishable within a take but shifted together across takes, drifting gradually with each performer moving from their own past as fast as from their partner's. In solo hand-offs, when one performer exceeded their own average surprise, the partner's next solo fell below their own, in both pitch and rhythm, in all duos.
AI.conclusion: Improvising pairs neither fuse into one system nor remain two independent ones: they keep individual melodic voices while sharing a rhythmic state, within which moment-to-moment push-pull rebalances the interaction. Individuality and togetherness coexist, carried by different musical dimensions—a measurable organization of creativity emerging between minds.

title: Generalized modeling reveals stabilizing mechanisms in cross-feeding microbial communities
summary: Understanding what makes microbial communities stable and able to resist perturbation is a fundamental question in microbial ecology. Theoretical approaches to this problem typically require making strict assumptions about the structure, parameters and functional forms used in models, hindering general insight. Here, we address this problem by developing and analyzing a generalized model of microbial community dynamics, capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions between populations. The generalized modeling approach allows us to assess the stability of microbial systems across large ensembles of models with variable size, structure and non-linear dynamics. Our analysis shows how community stability is constrained by system size and identifies its key metabolic and dynamical drivers, highlighting the central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency and plasticity. Furthermore, we show how the structure of communities mediates their stability, allowing communities to counteract the destabilizing cross-feeding loops through organization into hierarchical trophic structures. Together, these results provide new insight into the stability of microbial communities and offer a flexible analytical framework for future work to explore the responses of communities to perturbation.

AI.tldr: A generalized model of microbial community dynamics reveals that stability is constrained by system size and driven by self-limitation, metabolic efficiency, and plasticity, with hierarchical trophic organization counteracting destabilizing cross-feeding loops.
AI.motivation: Understanding microbial community stability and resistance to perturbation is fundamental, but existing theoretical approaches require strict assumptions about model structure, parameters, and functional forms, limiting general insight.
AI.method: The authors develop and analyze a generalized model of microbial community dynamics capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions. The generalized modeling approach assesses stability across large ensembles of models of variable size, structure, and non-linear dynamics.
AI.result: Community stability is constrained by system size. Key metabolic and dynamical drivers are identified, highlighting central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency, and plasticity. Community structure mediates stability, allowing communities to counteract destabilizing cross-feeding loops through hierarchical trophic organization.
AI.conclusion: The results offer new insight into microbial community stability and provide a flexible analytical framework for future work on community responses to perturbation.

title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
comment: 6 pages, presented at CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge
summary: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking synthetic scRNA-seq generators (scGFT, scLDM, Cell2Sentence) for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge shows that how non-HVG genes are handled—not the generator alone—dominates membership-inference leakage; Poisson reconstruction of non-HVGs preserves utility while cutting privacy risk.
AI.motivation: Donor-linked single-cell data cannot be shared freely, so synthetic data could enable privacy-aware sharing—but biological utility and privacy risk must be jointly balanced. Full-transcriptome generation is also computationally costly, and it is unclear how to handle non-highly-variable genes without leaking donor information.
AI.method: Using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, they restrict generative modeling to highly variable genes (HVGs), compare scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence plus an independent Poisson baseline, and test alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Evaluation covers statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability.
AI.result: Directly copying non-HVG values causes severe membership leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. scGFT and scLDM preserve biological structure better than the independent Poisson baseline and exhibit near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic single-cell data should be assessed beyond marginal similarity, with attention to robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious choices across preprocessing, generation, and post-processing; non-HVG handling is a central privacy determinant.

title: Dynamics of random recurrent neural networks: colored noise and sublinear activations
summary: We study the dynamics of recurrent neural networks with random couplings, sublinear odd activation functions, and temporally correlated noise. Using large N methods, we determine stationary correlations and distinguish the loss of local linear stability from the onset of chaos, characterized by a positive largest Lyapunov exponent. These thresholds delimit an intermediate regime in which local instability coexists with asymptotic stability under a common noise history. Their separation depends on both the noise correlation time and the asymptotic growth of the activation function. We show that internal noise with any finite correlation time cuts off the divergence of the network's intrinsic correlation time tau_corr at the edge of chaos; it exhibits a critical scaling tau_{corr,max} propto 1/sqrt{D_0}, where D_0 is the integrated noise strength. Static random input instead produces coincident thresholds and a divergent correlation time. We also calculate the frequency-dependent participation dimension from a four-point correlation function. Its zero-frequency value is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the network correlation time, predicting a smooth minimum at the weak-noise chaos threshold. Numerical simulations support the large-network predictions and reveal appreciable finite-size effects.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes random recurrent neural networks with sublinear odd activations and temporally correlated noise, distinguishing the loss of local linear stability from the onset of chaos and showing that any finite noise correlation time regularizes the diverging intrinsic correlation time at the chaos edge.
AI.motivation: Prior work on chaotic random RNNs often conflates local instability with true chaos (positive Lyapunov exponent), typically in noise-free or white-noise settings. The authors want to clarify these distinct thresholds and understand how temporally correlated noise and the activation's asymptotic growth shape the dynamics and correlation-time divergence near the edge of chaos.
AI.method: Large-N (mean-field) methods for random-coupling RNNs with sublinear odd activation functions and temporally correlated (colored) noise; computation of stationary two-point correlations, local linear stability, and largest Lyapunov exponent; analysis of the intrinsic correlation time tau_corr; and a frequency-dependent participation dimension derived from the four-point correlation function. Numerical simulations test the large-network predictions and finite-size effects.
AI.result: Local linear stability loss and chaos onset are separated, defining an intermediate regime of local instability with asymptotic stability under a common noise history; the separation depends on noise correlation time and activation growth. Internal noise with any finite correlation time cuts off the divergence of tau_corr at the chaos edge, with critical scaling tau_corr,max proportional to 1/sqrt(D0), where D0 is the integrated noise strength. Static random input instead yields coincident thresholds and a divergent correlation time. The zero-frequency participation dimension scales inversely with the fourth power of the network correlation time, predicting a smooth minimum at the weak-noise chaos threshold. Simulations confirm predictions and show sizeable finite-size effects.
AI.conclusion: Temporally correlated internal noise fundamentally regularizes the edge-of-chaos criticality of random RNNs, separating stability and chaos thresholds and bounding the correlation time with a universal 1/sqrt(D0) scaling, whereas static input preserves the sharp transition. Four-point participation dimension provides a diagnostic linking geometry, correlation time, and the weak-noise chaos threshold.

title: ProMORNA: An End-to-End Generative Framework for Full-Length mRNA Design
summary: Designing therapeutic messenger RNA (mRNA) requires generating full-length transcripts that optimally balance intracellular stability and translation efficiency. While generative models have advanced mRNA design, existing approaches rely on region-wise generation, expensive inference-time search, or target-specific model updates. To overcome these limitations, we introduce ProMORNA, a zero-shot, end-to-end generative framework for full-length mRNA design. ProMORNA aligns the design process with modern Large Language Model training pipelines: it utilizes a BART-style architecture pre-trained on over 6 million natural protein-mRNA pairs, followed by a two-stage post-training process comprising cold-start supervised fine-tuning and multi-objective reinforcement learning. By standardizing and aggregating relative advantages at the individual metric level with domain-specific stabilization, our post-training stage directly aligns the generative policy with conflicting biological constraints while avoiding direct scalarization of raw objective scores. In silico evaluations demonstrate that ProMORNA pushes the Pareto frontier of predicted stability and translation efficiency beyond standard baselines and GEMORNA, a leading state-of-the-art method. In three independent in vitro Fluc2P experiments, Candidate 2 achieved a 12-72h reporter-activity AUC 3.33 times that of the conventional Benchmark (Holm-adjusted $P=0.01285$), while its estimated 1.29-fold advantage over the reported best GEMORNA candidate remained exploratory. These results support ProMORNA as a promising framework for generating functionally active full-length mRNA candidates.

AI.tldr: ProMORNA is a zero-shot, end-to-end generative framework for full-length mRNA design that adapts LLM training pipelines (BART pretraining, cold-start SFT, multi-objective RL) to jointly optimize stability and translation efficiency.
AI.motivation: Therapeutic mRNA needs full-length transcripts balancing intracellular stability and translation efficiency. Existing generative approaches rely on region-wise generation, costly inference-time search, or target-specific model updates—limiting practicality and generalization.
AI.method: ProMORNA uses a BART-style architecture pre-trained on 6M+ natural protein-mRNA pairs, then two-stage post-training: cold-start supervised fine-tuning and multi-objective reinforcement learning. It standardizes/aggregates per-metric relative advantages with domain-specific stabilization, aligning the policy with conflicting biological constraints without scalarizing raw objective scores.
AI.result: In silico, ProMORNA extends the Pareto frontier of predicted stability and translation efficiency beyond baselines and the SOTA method GEMORNA. In three in vitro Fluc2P experiments, Candidate 2 reached a 12-72h reporter-activity AUC 3.33× the conventional Benchmark (Holm-adjusted P=0.01285); its 1.29-fold advantage over the reported best GEMORNA candidate remained exploratory.
AI.conclusion: ProMORNA is a promising framework for generating functionally active full-length mRNA candidates, though the advantage over GEMORNA needs more rigorous validation.

title: QProtFuse: Query-Guided Layer Fusion for Retrieval-Augmented Protein Function Prediction
summary: Predicting protein functions from amino acid sequences is essential to understanding biological processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible function descriptions to natural-language queries, yet their limited protein understanding motivates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing protein RAG methods primarily expand external retrieval signals while overlooking the rich knowledge encoded within a single protein language model (PLM). We show that retrieval performance varies across PLM layers and biological tasks, making conventional final-layer selection suboptimal. To this end, we propose QProtFuse, which uses queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein features and jointly learns protein and annotation retrieval through intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive objectives. On Prot-Inst-OOD, QProtFuse achieves the best protein and annotation retrieval scores, reaching 16.4\% Recall@1 with annotation reranking. These gains improve downstream RAG-based function descriptions, yielding the highest LLM-as-a-judge scores for both Qwen3-8B (6.22/10) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (6.68/10). Ablations and weight analyses demonstrate the value of query-guided fusion and complementary training objectives for exploiting a PLM's internal knowledge.

AI.tldr: QProtFuse improves protein function prediction RAG by using queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein language model features and jointly learning protein and annotation retrieval via intra- and cross-modal contrastive objectives.
AI.motivation: LLMs have limited protein understanding, motivating RAG; existing protein RAG methods focus on expanding external retrieval signals while ignoring the rich knowledge inside a single PLM. Retrieval performance varies across PLM layers and biological tasks, so conventional final-layer selection is suboptimal.
AI.method: QProtFuse uses queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein features and jointly learns protein and annotation retrieval through intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive objectives.
AI.result: On Prot-Inst-OOD, QProtFuse achieves the best protein and annotation retrieval scores, reaching 16.4% Recall@1 with annotation reranking, and improves downstream function descriptions, yielding top LLM-as-a-judge scores for Qwen3-8B (6.22/10) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (6.68/10). Ablations and weight analyses confirm the value of query-guided fusion and complementary training objectives.
AI.conclusion: Query-guided multi-layer fusion and joint protein-annotation contrastive learning effectively exploit a PLM's internal knowledge, improving both retrieval and downstream RAG-based protein function descriptions.

title: AI Mindmeld: A Latent Interconnect Protocol
summary:
LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training.
  The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility.
  Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld

AI.tldr: The authors propose "mindmeld": direct exchange of specialist representations (rather than text/images/etc.) into LLMs, via the Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP), which trains only connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states, enabling compositional, extensible, zero-shot cross-domain transfer.
AI.motivation: LLM scientific agents must bring specialist information into context, but current interfaces (text, images, audio, video) are a low-dimensional bottleneck relative to rich high-dimensional specialist representations. Direct representation exchange could convey more properties, including information an LLM would not think to request.
AI.method: LIP learns connectors that map specialist representations into LLM internal states, training only connectors while freezing all pretrained models. Three protein and three small-molecule specialists were connected to Gemma 3 (4B, 12B) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active). Connectors are trained independently, aiming for extensibility to new specialists, flexibility across questions/tasks, and compositionality without joint training.
AI.result: Independently trained connectors provide useful information without modifying the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. Zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks is demonstrated without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer.
AI.conclusion: Direct representation exchange is viable and scales with LLM capability, but limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained to treat specialist representations as native inputs, so access does not guarantee reliable interpretation, integration, or use in reasoning. The authors call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine, and reason with such inputs. Code, data, and pretrained connectors are released.

title: Non-Destructive Detection of Early Drought Stress via Spectral Submanifold Analysis
comment: Includes supplementary information and one supplementary video. This manuscript has been submitted
summary: Non-destructive early detection of water stress is critical for precision agriculture, yet current detection methods are often labor-intensive or destructive. We propose a rapid, non-invasive method based on Spectral Submanifold (SSM) reduction to analyze the nonlinear vibration dynamics of soybean plants. Unlike traditional linear modal analysis, our data-driven approach reveals a distinct transition in the dominant dynamics of the plant stem as drought progresses. Specifically, we uncover a sign reversal in the nonlinear damping coefficient within SSM-reduced models of full plants. Our finding reveals a fundamental transition in the plant's dissipative mechanics from a pressurized, fluid-rich vessel exhibiting superlinear (viscoelastic) damping to a dry, cellular solid dominated by sublinear (frictional) damping. This transition is closely correlated with the onset of physiological stress indicated by a significant decrease in the values of mature-leaf soil plant analysis development (SPAD) and colorimetric metrics. In contrast, traditional metrics, such as linear frequency and leaf wilting, do not provide consistent statistical signals of water stress. This study provides the first experimental evidence that SSM-based nonlinear model reduction can detect the changing internal state of a living organism, offering a physics-based metric for high-throughput plant phenotyping.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a rapid, non-invasive method using Spectral Submanifold (SSM) reduction to detect water stress in soybean plants by analyzing nonlinear stem vibration dynamics; they find a sign reversal in the nonlinear damping coefficient as drought progresses.
AI.motivation: Early detection of water stress is critical for precision agriculture, but existing methods are labor-intensive or destructive. Linear modal analysis and conventional metrics (linear frequency, leaf wilting) fail to give consistent statistical signals of water stress.
AI.method: A data-driven SSM-based nonlinear model reduction is applied to the vibration dynamics of full soybean plants, revealing a transition in the dominant stem dynamics; this is correlated with physiological stress indicators (SPAD values and colorimetric metrics).
AI.result: The nonlinear damping coefficient reverses sign during drought, indicating a shift from superlinear (viscoelastic) damping in pressurized, fluid-rich stems to sublinear (frictional) damping in dry, cellular solid stems. This transition correlates closely with onset of physiological stress (SPAD and colorimetric declines), whereas linear frequency and wilting show no consistent statistical signals.
AI.conclusion: This is the first experimental evidence that SSM-based nonlinear model reduction can detect the changing internal state of a living organism, offering a physics-based metric for high-throughput plant phenotyping.

title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
summary: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.

AI.tldr: Random train/test splits in protein classifiers cause phylogenetic leakage that inflates performance; under leave-one-taxon-out evaluation on venom compound classification, a persistent-homology graph neural network (PH-GNN) reaches 63.4% versus ~30% for a sequence-only baseline and 54-55% for other geometric priors.
AI.motivation: Reported 80-90% accuracies for classifying venom compounds by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+) do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa, because random splits allow models to exploit taxon-specific correlations via phylogenetic leakage. Taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, so cross-species prediction should be treated as a structured distribution shift requiring phylogenetically invariant representations.
AI.method: A shared multimodal backbone fusing ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network. Five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology) are compared under a leave-one-taxon-out protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds across five taxa. The persistent-homology variant (PH-GNN) encodes backbone geometry as topological descriptors robust to local structural perturbations.
AI.result: Under i.i.d. splits all models perform similarly (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, the sequence-only baseline drops to ~30%, other geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, and PH-GNN achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality. Topological (persistent-homology) representations are an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift, and phylogeny-aware protocols are necessary for trustworthy protein classifier benchmarks.

title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
summary: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

AI.tldr: DNA supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for DNA-protein co-condensation: protein wetting promotes twist-to-writhe conversion, and the resulting writhed conformations lower the nucleation barrier, enabling spontaneous condensation that otherwise remains kinetically trapped.
AI.motivation: DNA-protein co-condensation is central to genome compaction (heterochromatin, chromosome segregation), and transcription/replication continuously generate supercoiling, yet how torsional stress affects co-condensation is poorly understood.
AI.method: A theoretical/modeling approach coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, examining the interplay between supercoiling, twist-to-writhe conversion, and protein wetting.
AI.result: Protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, producing highly writhed DNA that promotes capillary collapse into protein-rich droplets. Without supercoiling, DNA stays kinetically trapped in metastable extended states; sufficient supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation.
AI.conclusion: Topology is established as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation, providing a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

title: RiboBridge: protein-conditioned de novo RNA binder structure design
summary: Designing RNA molecules that bind to target protein structures requires generating both an RNA conformation and its bound complex geometry, without assuming a predefined binding site. Existing approaches generally model these coupled processes within a unified representation, entangling RNA conformation generation with protein-relative placement. In this work, we introduce RiboBridge, a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein--RNA assembly through cross-frame interaction geometry. RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations within a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), and then predicts protein--RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independently defined RNA and protein coordinate frames. The resulting interaction geometry is converted into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose through rigid placement. We evaluate RiboBridge on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, and redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein--RNA complexes. Under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, where native information is used only after generation to select among already generated predicted-pocket candidates, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and the lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods. Component ablations and stage-wise diagnostics further characterize the contributions of RNA conformational generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, identifying the main sources of complex-recovery error.

AI.tldr: RiboBridge is a structure-first framework that decouples RNA conformational generation from protein-RNA assembly, using cross-frame interaction geometry to bind RNA to target protein structures without a predefined binding site.
AI.motivation: Designing RNA that binds target proteins requires jointly generating RNA conformation and bound-complex geometry without a known binding site; existing methods entangle conformation generation with protein-relative placement in a unified representation, which is problematic.
AI.method: RiboBridge proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations in a pretrained structural latent space (RiboSphere), predicts protein-RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independent RNA and protein coordinate frames, and converts the interaction geometry into a rigid, geometrically consistent protein-relative pose.
AI.result: Evaluated on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein-RNA complexes, using post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods; ablations and stage-wise diagnostics isolate contributions and error sources.
AI.conclusion: Separating RNA conformational generation from protein-RNA assembly via cross-frame interaction geometry is an effective strategy; component analyses clarify the roles of conformation generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, and identify the main sources of complex-recovery error.

title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
summary: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a "behavioral mapping" framework that uses the posterior of a coarse/higher-level model to filter parameter proposals for a detailed/lower-level model, learning a behavioral support level set via Gaussian processes to accelerate MCMC inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models.
AI.motivation: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is expensive due to repeated model simulation. Existing reduction-based acceleration typically requires state or parameter correspondence between models, which is restrictive. The authors aim to accelerate inference of a detailed model using information from a hierarchically related reduced model without needing such correspondence.
AI.method: Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, they define "behavioral compatibility" and quantify the behavioral support of detailed parameters using the reduced model posterior. They learn a level set of behavioral support with a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed-model parameter proposals before expensive simulations in MCMC. They also derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set preserves all detailed parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance.
AI.result: Applied to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data, the approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model after initial setup costs. Theoretical conditions guarantee the filtering retains data-compatible detailed parameters within a tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral mapping with GP-learned behavioral support provides a sound, correspondence-free way to accelerate Bayesian inference of detailed dynamical models using cheaper reduced-model posteriors, with provable retention guarantees and demonstrated speedups on gene-expression model hierarchy inference.

title: Global Convergence of Detailed Balanced Mass Action Systems
comment: 23 pages, 1 figure. Lean 4 formalization: https://github.com/BitMiracle-AI/detailed-balance-gac (tag v1.0). Use of AI tools is described in the Acknowledgements
summary: We give a self-contained proof that, for a finite detailed balanced mass-action system with positive rate constants, each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium and every positive trajectory converges to it, together with a Lean 4 formalization of the complete argument from persistence to convergence. Boundedness and persistence come from the barrier argument of OpenAI (2026) for weakly reversible systems: an arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation yields a finite-minimum barrier whose superlevel sets confine trajectories and give one logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state. The Horn-Jackson dissipation identity identifies the positive equilibria as an exponential family with parameters in the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace, which gives uniqueness in each class. A bounded-speed descent argument replaces LaSalle's invariance principle; it uses neither uniqueness of solutions nor continuous dependence on initial data, and it places every cluster point in that family. The route given here is direct and elementary, and its main theorem is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions. The proofs, the Lean development, and the manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness that packages a complete research environment: Claude Opus 5.5 made the research decisions, GPT 6 Astra carried them out, and the Lean kernel checked every formal step.

AI.tldr: A self-contained, elementary proof that finite detailed-balanced mass-action systems admit a unique positive equilibrium per stoichiometric compatibility class and that all positive trajectories converge to it, formalized end-to-end in Lean 4 and produced by an AI agent harness.
AI.motivation: Provide a direct, elementary route to the global attractivity theorem for detailed-balanced mass-action kinetics, avoiding heavier machinery (LaSalle invariance, uniqueness of solutions, continuous dependence on initial data), and demonstrate machine-checked verification of a full dynamical-systems argument.
AI.method: Boundedness and persistence via the OpenAI (2026) barrier argument for weakly reversible systems (arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation giving a finite-minimum barrier with superlevel sets; uniform logarithmic bound). Uniqueness of positive equilibria via the Horn-Jackson dissipation identity, identifying equilibria as an exponential family indexed by the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace. Convergence via a bounded-speed descent argument replacing LaSalle's invariance principle, placing every cluster point in that family. All steps formalized in Lean 4 against explicit definitions.
AI.result: Established: exactly one positive equilibrium per positive stoichiometric compatibility class; every positive trajectory converges to it; a uniform logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state; every cluster point lies in the exponential family of positive equilibria. The Lean kernel verifies the main theorem.
AI.conclusion: The global convergence theorem for detailed-balanced mass-action systems has a direct, elementary, and fully machine-checked proof, demonstrating that the complete argument from persistence to convergence can be formalized in Lean 4 and that AI agent harnesses (ClawsGO Science: Claude Opus 5.5 for decisions, GPT 6 Astra for execution) can produce kernel-verified research mathematics.
